content: Acute ear infections, also known as otitis media, are a common reason parents bring their children to the doctor. This condition involves inflammation and infection of the middle ear, which is located just behind the eardrum. Acute ear infections are typically short-lived but can be painful. Symptoms of Acute Ear Infections: In infants, the primary signs often include irritability and inconsolable crying. Many infants and children with an acute ear infection may also experience fever or difficulty sleeping. Tugging on the ear is not always a reliable indicator of an ear infection. In older children and adults, symptoms may include: Ear pain or earache A sensation of fullness in the ear General feelings of illness Vomiting Diarrhea Hearing loss in the affected ear The infection often begins shortly after a cold. Sudden drainage of yellow or green fluid from the ear may indicate a ruptured eardrum. All acute ear infections involve fluid accumulation behind the eardrum. Devices like electronic ear monitors (e.g., EarCheck) can detect this fluid at home, but a doctor’s confirmation is still necessary. Causes of Acute Ear Infections: The Eustachian tube, which connects the middle ear to the back of the throat, is responsible for draining fluid from the middle ear. If this tube becomes blocked, fluid can accumulate, creating an environment conducive to infection. Children are more prone to ear infections because their Eustachian tubes are more easily clogged. Contributing factors include: However, water entering the ear does not cause infections unless the eardrum is already perforated. Acute ear infections are more common in winter and are not contagious, though colds that lead to ear infections can spread among children. Risk Factors: Certain factors increase the likelihood of developing acute ear infections, such as: A healthcare provider will examine the ear using an otoscope. Signs of infection may include: Redness or dullness of the eardrum Air bubbles or fluid behind the eardrum Bloody fluid or pus in the middle ear A perforated eardrum If there is a history of recurrent ear infections, a hearing test may also be recommended. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: Contact a doctor if: Pain, fever, or irritability persists beyond 24 to 48 hours The child appears more ill than expected for an ear infection The child has a high fever or severe pain Severe pain suddenly subsides, which may indicate a ruptured eardrum Symptoms worsen or new symptoms develop, such as severe headache, dizziness, swelling around the ear, or facial muscle twitching For infants under six months, notify a doctor immediately if they develop a fever, even without other symptoms. Treatment Options: Many ear infections resolve without antibiotics. Pain management and allowing the body to heal naturally are often sufficient. Applying a warm cloth or water bottle to the affected ear Using over-the-counter or prescription ear drops for pain relief Taking over-the-counter medications like ibuprofen or acetaminophen for pain or fever (avoid aspirin in children) Children under six months with a fever or symptoms should see a doctor. Older children may be monitored at home if they do not have a fever above 102°F, severe pain, or other medical issues. If symptoms worsen or fail to improve, consult a healthcare provider to determine if antibiotics are necessary. Antibiotics: Ear infections can be caused by viruses or bacteria. Antibiotics are ineffective against viral infections and are not always prescribed for bacterial infections. However, children under six months with an ear infection are typically treated with antibiotics. Antibiotics are more likely to be prescribed if: The child is under two years old The child has a fever or appears very ill Symptoms do not improve within 24 to 48 hours It is crucial to complete the full course of antibiotics, even if symptoms improve. If there is no improvement within 48 to 72 hours, contact the doctor to discuss switching to a different antibiotic. Commonly prescribed antibiotics include amoxicillin, azithromycin, clarithromycin, cefdinir, cefuroxime, cefpodoxime, amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin), clindamycin, or ceftriaxone. Side effects may include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or, in rare cases, serious allergic reactions. For children with recurrent infections, a low daily dose of antibiotics may be prescribed to prevent new infections. Surgery: If infections persist despite treatment or if a child experiences frequent infections, ear tubes may be recommended. This procedure involves inserting a small tube into the eardrum to allow air to enter and fluid to drain. The procedure is performed under general anesthesia, and the tubes usually fall out on their own. If they do not, they can be removed in a doctor’s office. Enlarged adenoids may also be surgically removed if they contribute to recurrent infections. However, removing tonsils does not appear to help with ear infections. Prognosis: Acute ear infections are treatable but may recur. They can cause significant discomfort. If antibiotics are prescribed, it is essential to complete the full course as directed. Possible Complications: Most ear infections resolve without complications, though temporary hearing loss may occur due to lingering fluid in the ear. Rarely, more severe complications can develop, such as: Mastoiditis (infection of the skull bones) Meningitis (infection of the brain) Persistent fluid behind the eardrum (otitis media with effusion) Ruptured or perforated eardrum Chronic or recurrent ear infections Enlarged adenoids or tonsils Abscess or cyst formation (cholesteatoma) from chronic infections Speech or language delays in children with prolonged hearing loss Prevention: To reduce the risk of ear infections: Wash hands and toys frequently Choose daycare settings with fewer children (six or fewer) Avoid pacifiers Breastfeed, as it reduces the likelihood of ear infections; if bottle-feeding, hold the infant upright Avoid exposing children to secondhand smoke Ensure vaccinations are up-to-date, including the pneumococcal vaccine Avoid overusing antibiotics to prevent resistance
